description: The Stars🌟 is a team of six united by a love of space, data and building things that work. For NASA Space Apps 2026, we combined terrain analysis, machine learning and web development to create SpaceMirror, a platform that helps researchers find Earth locations that mirror Moon base sites. We shared the work across data processing, modelling, research, web development and design, and made every match transparent and easy to explore.
summary: SpaceMirror is a web platform that identifies places on Earth whose terrain mirrors permanent Moon base locations. Using NASA LOLA lunar elevation data and SRTM Earth data, we measure slope, roughness, relief, pit and cave potential, and sunlight exposure for each site. We then score 14 Earth candidates against eight lunar targets with a weighted similarity index and publish the results in an interactive map where users can re-weight priorities, filter sites and read a detailed dossier for each match. This addresses the challenge by giving mission planners an evidence-based shortlist of places to test rovers, landers and habitats before Artemis missions. It matters because Moon testing is impossible in advance, and well-matched Earth analogs reduce risk and cost. The design extends to Mars by adding Mars targets from a Mars elevation model.
details:
What it does. SpaceMirror (TL-TDE, the Terrestrial-Lunar Topological Discovery Engine) finds places on Earth whose terrain matches candidate Moon base and landing sites, so rovers, landers and habitats can be tested on Earth before flying. It reads NASA’s LOLA lunar elevation model and USGS SRTM(NASAEDM) 30 m Earth tiles. Both are converted to real metres, so slopes and heights are directly comparable between the two worlds. For each terrain patch it measures slope (Horn gradient), roughness (detrended RMS and Vector Ruggedness Measure), local relief, pit depth and cave-shielding potential, and a solar-illumination proxy. Every Earth site is then scored against eight lunar targets (including Mare Tranquillitatis Pit, Marius Hills, Shackleton, Malapert and Mons Mouton) with a weighted similarity index: 30% slope, 25% roughness, 20% relief, 15% cave/subsurface, 10% solar. The result is a ranked catalog of 14 Earth analogs in Egypt, Brazil, the USA and Canada, shown in an interactive web app.

Benefits and impact. Mission planners get a transparent shortlist of test sites, with the evidence behind each match (side-by-side metrics, landing-safety category, lithology, caveats). Users can re-weight priorities live, for example valuing caves over slope, and the ranking updates instantly. The app is free to host and needs no API keys.

Tools. Python (NumPy, SciPy, pandas, matplotlib) for processing, and HTML/CSS/JavaScript for the app, with Leaflet maps, Esri/OSM/USGS basemaps and three.js globes.

Creativity. Our web is one of a kind making tying equipment trial before moon launch easier on scientists and junior scientist.
We add cave and lava-tube metrics and polar illumination to classic slope/roughness matching. The web app lets the user decide what “similar” means, and it is built so Mars targets can be added later.

Factors considered. Planet radius and latitude distortion of grid cells, voids and laser speckle in the data, log-scale comparison of roughness and relief, and the limits of terrain-only matching. Gravity, vacuum and regolith are not modeled, and the app displays an environmental caveat for each site.
dataRefs: The Earth elevation tiles: NASADEM 1 arc-second (~30 m) tiles such as s01w047.hgt, plus the .num and .swb companion files, and the other tiles for Egypt, USA and Canada
The Moon elevation model: LRO LOLA global DEM ldem_16_float.img (16 pixels per degree, float32, kilometres
